items.title: Koulpélogo/Ouargaye : le Directeur régional de la Famille et de la Solidarité salue l’engagement des acteurs sur le terrain
items.description: BURKINA-AUTORITE-ENCOURAGEMENT-PERSONNEL-DIRECTION-FAMILLE-KOULPELOGO Koulpélogo/Ouargaye : le Directeur régional de la Famille et de la Solidarité salue l’engagement des acteurs sur le terrain Ouargaye, 12 septembre 2026 (AIB) – Le Directeur régional de la Famille et de la Solidarité du Nakambé, Boukaré Zabsonré, a effectué une visite de travail et d’encouragement à Ouargaye, vendredi 11 septembre 2026. Objectif, soutenir l’ensemble des agents de ce bureau qui se sont engagés dans l’accompagnement des populations, malgré le contexte sécuritaire et humanitaire difficile. À son arrivée, le Directeur régional a été reçu par le Haut-commissaire de la province du Koulpélogo, Saïdou Ouédraogo. Les échanges ont porté sur la situation humanitaire et les actions menées par les services sociaux au profit des populations vulnérables. Le camarade Zabsonré s’est ensuite rendu à la Cour royale de Ouargaye, où il a rencontré les autorités coutumières. Il leur a exprimé sa reconnaissance, compte tenu de leur contribution au maintien de la cohésion sociale ainsi que leurs efforts en faveur du retour de la paix dans la province. La visite s’est poursuivie auprès des Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et des Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP), notamment au siège des VDP, à la Direction provinciale de la Police et à la Gendarmerie. Ces rencontres ont permis à l’autorité de saluer l’engagement des forces combattantes pour la sécurisation et la reconquête du territoire. Lors de sa tournée, le Directeur régional a également suivi une opération de distribution de vivres du Conseil national de secours d’urgence et de réhabilitation (CONASUR). Une remise de moustiquaires a également été faite au profit de trois catégories de bénéficiaires : les personnes déplacées internes (PDI), celles qui se sont réinstallées dans leur communauté d’origine ainsi que les populations hôtes vulnérables. Les acteurs rencontrés ont salué le travail accompli par l’équipe de la Direction provinciale de la Famille et de la Solidarité (DPFS) du Koulpélogo, notamment les efforts consentis pour maintenir l’accompagnement social des citoyens dans un contexte particulièrement difficile. Prenant la parole à l’issue de la visite, le Directeur provincial de la Famille et de la Solidarité du Koulpélogo, le camarade Wendingoudi Justin Tiendrébeogo, a exprimé sa joie d’accueillir le Directeur régional à Ouargaye. « Il a fait l’effort de nous rendre visite malgré le contexte sécuritaire », s’est-il réjoui. Pour lui, cette mission a également permis à leur hôte de constater les avancées enregistrées sur le terrain, en l’occurrence le retour de nombreuses personnes déplacées internes dans leurs localités d’origine. « Ce résultat est le fruit des efforts conjugués des FDS et des VDP », a-t-il souligné. Le camarade Wendingoudi Justin Thiendrébeogo a par ailleurs témoigné sa profonde gratitude au Directeur régional pour son soutien constant. « Vos conseils avisés ainsi que vos directives nous ont permis de renforcer les acquis pour un meilleur accompagnement des populations, particulièrement celles retournées dans les zones reconquises », a-t-il ajouté. Une rencontre d’échanges avec le personnel de la DPFS s’est tenue dans la salle de réunion de la direction. C’était l’occasion, pour le chef de la région, de recueillir les préoccupations des agents, de s’imprégner davantage des réalités du terrain et de partager des orientations pour consolider l’efficacité des interventions sociales. À travers cette visite, le camarade Boukaré Zabsonré a ainsi marqué son soutien au personnel de cette administration qui, dans un contexte sécuritaire et humanitaire exigeant, poursuivent leurs missions d’assistance et de protection des publics vulnérables. Agence d'Information du Burkina BP/ata/zs

items.title: Ghana’s Ambassador to Serbia hosts African ambassadors’ September meeting in Belgrade
items.description: Ghana’s Ambassador to Serbia, Kwesi Ahwoi, has hosted the September 2026 meeting of the Group of African Ambassadors resident in Serbia. The meeting, held at the Ghana Mission’s Residence in Belgrade, brought together African ambassadors and other diplomatic representatives stationed in Serbia to discuss issues of common interest to the African diplomatic community. The regular gathering provides a platform for African diplomatic missions in Serbia to exchange views on developments affecting the continent and explore opportunities for closer cooperation. It also allows the ambassadors to coordinate their engagements and strengthen diplomatic and professional ties among African countries represented in Serbia. Ambassador Ahwoi’s hosting of the September meeting highlights Ghana’s active participation in the African diplomatic community in Belgrade and its efforts to promote closer relations among African missions. Beyond the formal discussions, the gathering also provided an opportunity for the diplomats to interact in a more informal setting, with Ghana showcasing aspects of its culture and hospitality. Ghanaian hospitality Following the meeting, Ambassador Ahwoi hosted his colleagues to a selection of Ghanaian delicacies. The meal offered the visiting ambassadors an opportunity to sample traditional Ghanaian cuisine while engaging in informal conversations after the official proceedings. The presentation of Ghanaian food also served as an avenue for cultural diplomacy, allowing Ghana to showcase part of its culinary heritage to representatives of other African countries. Such informal engagements can complement formal diplomatic discussions by helping to build stronger personal relationships and foster greater cooperation among diplomats. The September meeting forms part of the regular engagements of African ambassadors resident in Serbia, providing an avenue for consultation and coordination on issues of shared interest. Ghana’s participation in the group also forms part of its broader diplomatic engagement with Serbia and other countries in the European region. The hosting of the meeting by Ambassador Ahwoi, coupled with the display of Ghanaian hospitality, therefore brought together diplomatic consultation and cultural exchange, reinforcing the spirit of cooperation among African missions in Belgrade.

items.title: Casablanca: Opération de retour volontaire de 137 migrants soudanais vers leur pays d'origine
items.description: Une opération de retour volontaire de 137 migrants soudanais en situation irrégulière vers leur pays d'origine a été réalisée, vendredi, au départ de l'aéroport international Mohammed V de Casablanca, par les autorités marocaines en coordination avec l'ambassade du Soudan au Maroc. Cette opération s'inscrit dans le cadre de la politique marocaine de migration et d'asile, basée sur une approche humaniste et qui repose sur le respect des droits et de la dignité des migrants, en application des Hautes Directives du Roi Mohammed VI, que Dieu L’assiste. Outre la régularisation de la situation de dizaines de milliers de migrants, cette stratégie a offert l'opportunité à des milliers de ceux qui souhaitent regagner leurs pays d'origine, à travers des opérations de retour volontaire. Dans une déclaration à la MAP, l’ambassadrice du Soudan au Maroc, Mawada Omar Hageltoam El Badawi, s’est félicitée de ce premier vol de retour volontaire de migrants soudanais désireux de regagner leur pays afin de contribuer aux efforts de reconstruction et de développement. Mme El Badawi a exprimé, en son nom et au nom du gouvernement soudanais, ses sincères remerciements et sa profonde gratitude à Sa Majesté le Roi Mohammed VI, ainsi qu’au gouvernement et au peuple marocains, pour les facilités accordées en vue de la réussite de cette opération. Cette initiative, a-t-elle souligné, n’aurait pas pu être concrétisée sans l’appui des autorités marocaines, qui veillent à la mise en œuvre de la vision éclairée de Sa Majesté le Roi, fondée sur la coopération Sud-Sud et le renforcement des partenariats africains. Mettant en l’expérience marocaine en matière de migration, fondée notamment sur la dimension humaine et les principes de solidarité, elle a affirmé que cette approche s’impose comme un modèle à suivre par les pays africains. La diplomate a, par ailleurs, salué les conditions d’accueil au Maroc des ressortissants soudanais qui ont toujours bénéficié d’un traitement digne et d’une hospitalité exemplaire de la part des autorités et du peuple marocains, ce qui reflète la profondeur des relations historiques, fraternelles et culturelles unissant les deux pays. Dans une déclaration similaire, Youssef, un migrant soudanais bénéficiant de cette opération de retour volontaire, a exprimé sa profonde gratitude envers le Maroc, Roi, gouvernement et peuple, pour l’accueil qui leur a été réservé. « Nous remercions vivement Sa Majesté le Roi, le gouvernement et le peuple marocains pour l’accueil chaleureux qu’ils nous ont accordé», a-t-il déclaré, tout en saluant les efforts déployés par les autorités marocaines pour «faciliter notre retour au Soudan, afin de contribuer à sa reconstruction et à son développement ». The post Casablanca: Opération de retour volontaire de 137 migrants soudanais vers leur pays d'origine appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Gnagna : 25 jeunes de Coalla renforcent leurs compétences en entrepreneuriat
items.description: BURKINA-GNAGNA-FORMATION-ENTREPRENEURIAT-JEUNES Gnagna : 25 jeunes de Coalla renforcent leurs compétences en entrepreneuriat Bogandé, 11 septembre 2026 (AIB) – Vingt-cinq jeunes de la commune de Coalla, dans la province de la Gnagna, region de la Sirba, ont renforcé, les 10 et 11 septembre 2026 au Haut-commissariat de Bogandé, leurs compétences en entrepreneuriat. C’était à la faveur d’une session initiée par le service Referent-Opportunités-Insertion des jeunes de ladite commune, avec l’appui de la Direction provinciale de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi de la Gnagna (DPJE/Gnagna). Pendant deux jours, les participants ont été outillés sur plusieurs thématiques, notamment les notions de base en entrepreneuriat, le montage de plans d’affaires, la communication marketing et les mécanismes de financement des projets. La formation a été assurée par le directeur provincial de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi de la Gnagna, Abdoulaye Sanogo, qui a privilégié une approche participative, alternant exposés, échanges, questions-réponses et travaux pratiques en groupe. Selon le président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de Coalla, Abdourazac Gansoré, cette initiative vise à développer le sens des affaires chez les jeunes, stimuler leur esprit d’entreprise et faciliter leur insertion professionnelle. Il a ainsi encouragé les bénéficiaires à mettre en pratique les connaissances acquises pour créer leurs propres activités et, à terme, générer des emplois pour d’autres jeunes. « C’est avec une grande joie que nous avons reçu cette formation et nous prenons l’engagement de mettre ses nouvelles compétences au service de l’employabilité », a déclaré le représentant des bénéficiaires, Ouaboa Djingri . Le PDS de Coalla a, par ailleurs, rassuré les jeunes de la disponibilité de la commune à les accompagner dans les démarches administratives liées à la formalisation de leurs projets, notamment l’obtention de l’Identifiant financier unique (IFU) et du Registre du commerce et du crédit mobilier (RCCM). Cette session s’inscrit dans la volonté des autorités communales de Coalla de promouvoir l’entrepreneuriat et l’autonomisation économique des jeunes, considérés comme des acteurs essentiels du développement local. Agence d'information du Burkina AYT/ata/zs

items.title: Kintinian : il arrache le sac d’une passagère, le conducteur de taxi-moto le poursuit pendant plus de 30 mn et le fait arrêter
items.description: Un acte de braquage d’une rare violence s’est produit dans la nuit du vendredi 11 septembre 2026, aux environs de 22 heures, dans le secteur de Kankankoura, relevant de la zone de Boukaria, dans la commune urbaine de Kintinian. Un jeune homme a violemment arraché le sac à main d’une passagère installée sur une moto-taxi alors que celle-ci était en pleine circulation. Projetée au sol sous l’effet du choc, la victime a été grièvement blessée. Selon nos informations, le suspect aurait ciblé l’épaule de la dame pendant que la moto était en mouvement. La violence de l’arrachage a déséquilibré la passagère, qui a lourdement chuté. Dans le sac emporté par le présumé malfrat se trouvaient un téléphone Android ainsi qu’une somme de quatre millions soixante mille francs guinéens (4 060 000 GNF). Loin de céder à la panique, le conducteur de la moto-taxi a immédiatement pris en chasse le présumé bandit. Une course-poursuite intense s’est alors engagée dans les rues de la localité pendant plus d’une demi-heure, jusqu’à Bouré Köfilani, où le fuyard a finalement été rattrapé. Bien qu’il ait accepté de nous confier son identité, le courageux conducteur a souhaité s’exprimer sous couvert d’anonymat visuel, exigeant que son image ne soit pas publiée pour des raisons de sécurité. Il revient sur le moment crucial de l’arrestation, au cours duquel le suspect aurait tenté de retourner la situation contre lui : « Lorsque j’ai réussi à intercepter et arrêter le présumé bandit, ce dernier a tenté de retourner la situation contre moi. Il s’est mis à crier de toutes ses forces en me pointant du doigt et en hurlant : “Au voleur ! Au voleur !”, juste pour induire la population en erreur », a-t-il confié à notre micro. Face à cette tentative de manipulation qui aurait pu lui coûter cher, le conducteur dit avoir gardé son sang-froid : « Je me suis expliqué rapidement et clairement devant les personnes qui commençaient déjà à s’assembler. Très fort heureusement, la population a tout de suite compris la situation », a-t-il laissé entendre, les larmes aux yeux et remerciant Dieu. Grâce à cette proactivité, le fuyard a finalement été maîtrisé. Afin d’éviter tout débordement ou risque de justice populaire, le suspect a d’abord été conduit auprès du chef de quartier local. Il a ensuite été transféré et mis à la disposition du commissariat de police de Bouré Boukaria, dans la commune urbaine de Kintinian, qui a ouvert une procédure d’enquête. Les autorités policières ont également demandé que l’image du suspect ne soit pas diffusée afin de ne pas compromettre les investigations en cours. La victime, quant à elle, a été prise en charge pour ses blessures. Cet événement relance le débat sur la sécurité des passagers et des conducteurs de deux-roues pendant la nuit dans la préfecture de Bouré-Kintinian. Oubri : le bilan de l’opération WIBGA 3 affiche plus de 71 000 engins contrôlés et 76 interpellations
items.description: BURKINA-RESULTATS-CONTROLE-SECURITE-ENGIN-REGION-OUBRI Oubri : le bilan de l’opération WIBGA 3 affiche plus de 71 000 engins contrôlés et 76 interpellations Ziniaré, 10 septembre 2026 (AIB) – La Police nationale a contrôlé 66 335 personnes et 71 439 engins dans la région d’Oubri, du 9 juillet au 31 août 2026, dans le cadre de l’opération « WIBGA 3 ». Le bilan fait également état de 76 interpellations, ainsi que de plusieurs saisies d’armes, de stupéfiants, de produits illicites et de documents frauduleux. Le bilan à mi-parcours de la mission a été transmis à la presse le 10 septembre 2026. Au total, 402 policiers ont été mobilisés dans la région d’Oubri, où 339 patrouilles et actions communautaires ont été menées au cours de la période indiquée. Les interventions ont porté sur le contrôle des personnes et des véhicules. Les forces de sécurité ont inspecté 47 551 motos, 4 356 tricycles et 19 532 automobiles, soit 71 439 moyens de transport au total. Deux cent soixante-cinq d’entre eux ont été saisis et 3 477 500 francs CFA d’amendes forfaitaires ont été enregistrés. Sur le volet judiciaire, 76 usagers de la route ont été interpellées. Trente-trois ont été placés en garde à vue et 20 ont été déférés. Les opérations ont également permis de mettre la main sur plusieurs armes. Il s’agit notamment de deux fusils AK-47 avec deux chargeurs et 48 munitions, d’un pistolet automatique et de 13 munitions, ainsi que de dix armes blanches et d’un couteau-baïonnette. Les services de police ont par ailleurs confisqué 250 kg de cyanure, sept bidons d’essence de 20 litres, 25 kg de Tramadol estimés à 7 500 000 francs CFA et 95 cartons de produits périmés. Cinq faux permis de conduire et divers documents administratifs ont également été interceptés. Une moto déclarée volée a été retrouvée et un véhicule Range Rover saisi. Selon le bilan, aucun incident sécuritaire majeur n’a été enregistré dans le ressort de la Direction régionale de la Police nationale d’Oubri durant la période considérée. L’opération « WIBGA 3 », lancée officiellement le 8 juillet 2026 par le ministre de la Sécurité, Mahamadou Sana, se poursuit. La Police nationale invite les populations à signaler tout fait suspect aux numéros verts 16, 17 et 1010. Agence d'information du Burkina LC/ata/zs

items.title: Tens of thousands protest against far right in Germany
items.description: Tens of thousands of protesters took part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday against the far-right AfD, after the party scored a crushing victory in a state election last week. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) topped the vote in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt, and is now seeking to form the first extreme-right state government in Germany since World War II. About 150,000 demonstrators took to the streets in around 20 cities nationwide, including Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, in protests that were called by Pruef, which advocates for a ban on the AfD, organisers said. They waved signs emblazoned with slogans that read “Ban the AfD now,” and “Democracy needs no alternatives”. A counter-protester holds a sign reading “Who replaces remigrated caregivers” during a final election campaign rally of far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party ahead of Berlin’s state election in Germany on September 12, 2026. — AFP “A broad cross-section of civil society is taking to the streets to prevent the enemies of the constitution, the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, from gaining government power,” said Christoph Bautz, head of campaign group Campact, also involved in the demonstrations. The rise of the AfD has unnerved many who feel Germany has a special responsibility to atone for its Nazi past, and calls have grown for mainstream parties to seek to ban the group. But hurdles for a formal ban are high in Germany, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, of the centre-right CDU party, remains sceptical about taking such an approach. In Berlin, police said several thousand protesters took part in several demonstrations. The AfD held a counter-demonstration in the capital, attended by Kristin Brinker, its lead candidate in next weekend’s regional elections in Berlin. Campact said there were around 25,000 demonstrators in Hamburg and 12,000 in Munich. The anti-immigration, Russia-friendly party took almost 44 per cent of the vote in last Sunday’s election in Saxony-Anhalt, against 17pc for the CDU. It fell three seats short of an absolute majority and has started talks with other groups and MPs in an effort to form a state government.

items.title: Egypt prepares to launch clinical trials for Ebola vaccine
items.description: Scientists in Egypt are working to strengthen protection against Ebola, with clinical trials for a new vaccine expected to begin in the coming weeks. The development follows a decision by the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) to support Egypt's Minapharm in advancing the vaccine. Minapharm operates what it describes as the largest biologics manufacturing facility in the Middle East and Africa. The company is developing the vaccine with its Germany-based subsidiary, ProBioGen. Dr. Ashraf Omar, Professor of Hepatology and Liver Transplantation, says the project demonstrates Egypt's growing capacity in vaccine development and clinical research. "It has a very significant impact, because it's a positive vote, that Egypt is capable of having the biotechnology of producing vaccines," Omar said. He added that Africa accounts for less than 2% of clinical trials globally, making the project an opportunity to position Egypt as a hub for clinical research. Minapharm and ProBioGen launched the vaccine development program following the outbreak of the latest deadly Ebola strain, for which there is currently no known vaccine or treatment. CEPI is providing about $16.5 million to help advance the vaccine from pre-clinical development to Phase One clinical trials. The funding covers manufacturing in Cairo and Berlin, as well as pre-clinical and regulatory work, the Phase One trial and technology transfer between the two facilities, according to Minapharm's Head of Biologics Pipeline, Mohamed Youssef. "We are moving extremely fast on this. We are planning for manufacturing of the first batch in just a few weeks, then we proceed with the first human clinical trials in Rwanda," Youssef said. Minapharm says the first human trials involving volunteers in Rwanda are planned for December. If the vaccine receives the necessary regulatory approvals, a public rollout could begin in early 2027.

items.title: Ghana closer to terrorism threat than ever before – WACCE
items.description: The West Africa Centre for Counter-Extremism (WACCE) has warned that Ghana faces a growing terrorism threat as extremist violence spreads across the Sahel and closer to the country’s borders. The Centre says Ghana’s geographical proximity to countries experiencing increasing extremist attacks, coupled with internal socioeconomic challenges, could make the country more vulnerable to violent extremism. Speaking at a 9/11 Memorial Dialogue in Accra on Thursday, September 11, WACCE Executive Director Mutaru Mumuni Muqthar said Ghana was now “closer to the threat” than ever before. “We are closer to the threat than ever. If you look at the geographical proximity, we are closer to the threat now than we have ever been,” he said. Mr Muqthar noted that terrorism was previously viewed largely as a distant threat from countries such as Mali, but the situation had changed significantly, particularly with the spread of extremist violence in Burkina Faso. “Before 2014, we didn’t have terrorism in Burkina Faso. It was seen as a distant threat in Mali and other parts of West Africa. Today, the attacks are closer to our borders,” he said. He also pointed to the movement of people fleeing insecurity in Burkina Faso and other affected areas as another factor Ghana must consider in assessing its security risks. Internal vulnerabilities Mr Muqthar said geographical proximity was only one part of the challenge. He identified unemployment, economic insecurity, prolonged conflicts, chieftaincy disputes and ethnic tensions as internal vulnerabilities that could potentially be exploited by extremist groups. “The issues of pervasive unemployment involving young people, prolonged disputes, conflict, chieftaincy disputes, ethnic disputes—all of these are factors that could be exploited by extremist groups,” he cautioned. “These, put together, make us more vulnerable than we have ever been,” he added. The warning comes against the backdrop of a changing global terrorism landscape, with the Sahel emerging as a major centre of extremist violence. The 2025 Global Terrorism Index identifies the Sahel as the epicentre of terrorism globally, with the region accounting for more than half of terrorism-related deaths worldwide. Call for stronger community resilience WACCE is urging the government to increase investment in youth empowerment and strengthen community-based approaches to preventing and countering violent extremism. The Centre said addressing socioeconomic vulnerabilities, particularly among young people, would be critical to building resilience in communities that could otherwise become susceptible to extremist recruitment and influence. It said a stronger community-based response, alongside efforts to address unemployment and local conflicts, would help Ghana better prepare for emerging extremist threats and protect vulnerable communities.

items.title: AI Is Running Laps Around Our Political System
items.description: P oliticians have no shortage of ideas about how to rein in AI: a 100 percent federal tax rate on data-center incentives, a pause on all development of advanced AI, new standards to block AI agents from going rogue, a halt to the construction of data centers altogether. The flurry of proposals has been impossible to miss, with both Democrats and Republicans proclaiming that something must be done to avert a disaster foretold by AI insiders. Current and former Anthropic researchers have in recent days gone public with warnings that AI could wipe out humanity before the decade ends; the company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, wrote in an essay today that the industry must “slow the pace” at which the technology is being developed. Meanwhile, OpenAI agents escaped a test environment and conspired with one another to breach the servers of the AI giant Hugging Face , an incident that caused alarm both in Silicon Valley and on Capitol Hill. Politicians are also dealing with mounting public opposition to data centers and the fear that robots will soon replace humans across large swaths of the workforce. If this were an alien-invasion movie, now would be the moment when people of all persuasions put aside their differences and band together to save the human race. But that kind of bonhomie feels far out of reach. Instead, technological advances and grassroots sentiment have been moving faster than politicians have been willing to act. Now some seem to be waking up. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Republican, said last Wednesday that he will soon unveil legislation, alongside Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, intended to head off AI-induced biological or nuclear catastrophes. Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a Democrat, and Representative Mike Lawler of New York, a Republican, teamed up earlier this month to introduce legislation that would direct the federal government to create standards for securely deploying AI agents and preventing them from going rogue. Several lawmakers have called for Congress to reconvene specifically for the purpose of addressing the threats posed by AI. Yesterday, Representative Ro Khanna, who represents part of Silicon Valley, called for the creation of an AI safety agency. Others are shifting their position in real time. Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, released a lengthy plan in June for AI development to continue with greater regulation and restrictions. He said Wednesday that he now favors “an all-out pause” on AI development. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who once approvingly called the state “the epicenter of AI development,” ordered an audit of all data-center projects before any could move forward. But whether politicians can act quickly enough to mitigate possible damage is doubtful, experts told me. “The developments are coming so fast and furious that it is very difficult to keep up with what the harms are and how to address them,” Nate Persily, a co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, told me. He said that although there’s a growing consensus that it would be “foolish” to allow AI to continue advancing without robust federal guardrails, the complexities and rapidly changing threat landscape would challenge any country’s leadership. “There are genuinely hard questions of statutory design here,” he said. The next few weeks—and the upcoming elections—could determine whether or not politicians are able to deliver any meaningful results or whether they will instead default to the partisan gridlock that most Americans now expect. “The good news is that people across the political spectrum are understanding that we have a technology which is the most dangerous and transformational in human history,” Senator Bernie Sanders told me. The Vermont democratic socialist was among the first lawmakers to call for a moratorium on the data centers that facilitate AI advancement and for a broader pause on the industry’s growth. We spoke shortly after Sanders sent out an invitation to members of Congress for a closed-door briefing this week with top AI-safety experts. The briefing, which will take place on Wednesday, is designed to give lawmakers a clearer understanding of the threats posed by AI and ideas for legislative action. The invitation was made especially timely by a Tuesday social-media post from the AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who wrote that he had resigned from Anthropic over concerns about the risks of the fast-advancing technology. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Coxon, a former employee of both OpenAI and Anthropic. His posts, which argue that the AI industry is “gambling with our lives,” were publicly boosted by several other AI researchers. The messages seemed to break through in a way that few other warnings have. Sanders told me that Coxon’s X post, which received more than 120 million views within 24 hours, landed among his colleagues in Congress as “an extraordinary wake-up call.” P resident Trump’s signature will be needed to enact any significant change to federal AI policy, but so far, he’s not among those who seem particularly worried. As concerns about AI and data centers have proliferated, Trump has said “let Data Reign” and rejected calls to restrict AI development in the United States. His former AI czar took a similar laissez-faire approach, espousing a philosophy that he summarized as “ let the private sector cook .” Some other Republicans are also wary of saddling American AI companies with too much government oversight. Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said earlier this year that her proposed TRUMP AMERICA AI Act, which aims to codify the president’s pro-industry executive order on artificial intelligence, would “ensure America triumphs over foreign adversaries in the global race for AI dominance.” Even for those Republicans who do believe in more muscular federal guardrails for tech companies, Trump’s position presents a significant political hurdle. The president has made clear that he does not want regulation to impede America’s ability to win the global AI race. As is his custom, he has shown no hesitation about attacking members of his own coalition who disagree with him. Even as a growing number of Republican lawmakers are embracing some limits on AI and data centers, few have been willing to openly cross Trump or sign on to more sweeping legislation to pause or restrict AI advancement. In recent years, America’s polarized political system has generated bitter stalemates on how to prevent school shootings, what to do about climate change, and where to draw the line in responding to a once-in-a-generation pandemic. The question of how to handle the race toward superintelligence might not be any different. In July, about 1,400 AI-company employees signed an open letter calling on the government to help regulate their industry. In a nearly 6,000-word essay published last month, the Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates wrote that powerful AI models “could begin to act against our interests and we could lose control.” In a report published Thursday, Anthropic said that it had intervened to stop several attempts by scientists to use its models in a way that could potentially help develop biological weapons. Amodei wrote that he worries that within the next 6 to 12 months, a swarm of models similar to the one that breached the Hugging Face servers “could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.” AI, of course, has already delivered advances in health care and science, and there’s no consensus on the scale of the threat it poses. Nuance is required to figure out how to manage it. But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle acknowledge that our current political landscape does not lend itself to sober, cross-party problem-solving. “It is possible to move bipartisan legislation,” Cruz said on ABC’s The View Wednesday after discussing the prospects of his proposed bill. He added, “But it ain’t easy. This is a very divided time.” So far, none of the recent AI-related legislation appears close to becoming law. A bill proposed by Sanders and Representative Greg Casar of Texas, which would ban superintelligence and pause advanced-AI development, faces long odds because no Republicans have signed on. Democratic and Republican political strategists I spoke with said that the likelihood of bipartisan cooperation to properly govern AI is slim at best. “People are deeply cynical and deeply skeptical, and then you add into that this moment of severe economic disruption,” Joel Payne, a Democratic strategist, told me. “The politicization and the polarization is lighter fluid on top of that.” That these warnings about AI are emerging in the heat of election season only heightens the likelihood of inaction. With Congress largely out of session for the rest of the year, politicians have settled into campaign mode, attempting to reposition themselves politically and outflank their opponents. In Wisconsin, the race for governor has been dominated by political posturing over data centers. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor, has run ads branding his Democratic opponent, David Crowley, as “Data Center David Crowley.” The Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has run television ads blasting the incumbent, Jon Husted, as “the face of data centers in Ohio.” A memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that data centers are “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck” that could ultimately cause him to lose in a state that Trump won handily in 2024. Crowley and Husted have responded with attacks of their own, attempting to link their opponents to data-center development. Political-ad spending nationwide on spots highlighting data centers has spiked in recent months; both Democrats and Republicans have spent millions to attack opponents on the issue, according to data from the firm AdImpact. Tech companies have also poured millions of dollars into political-action committees with the aim of boosting candidates who are friendlier to their cause. Virginia has become central to this effort. Loudoun County, not far from Washington, D.C., has the largest concentration of data centers in the world, and advocates have tried to tout the benefits for the economy and tax revenue even as residents have raised quality-of-life concerns. The Data Center Coalition, whose membership includes Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, has recently stepped up lobbying efforts in D.C. and in Northern Virginia to oppose moratoriums on data centers and stricter regulations at the federal, state, and local levels. “Sweeping restrictions do not solve complex infrastructure challenges; instead, they risk stalling economic opportunity, defunding essential local public services, and undermining America’s technological edge,” Nicole Riley, the director of Virginia government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, told me. The White House has shown little interest in halting the march of advanced AI. Trump attacked data-center detractors late last month, posting on social media that communities should oppose the projects only “if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” In May, Trump intervened to postpone an executive order aimed at regulating AI development, telling reporters that “we’re leading China. We’re leading everybody, and I don’t want to do anything that’s going to get in the way of that lead.” The president later signed a narrower order that allows developers to engage governmental review of advanced AI models before their release. “President Trump’s bold leadership is turning data centers into engines of growth and opportunity for communities across the country that want them, all while cementing America’s dominance over China in the global AI race,” the White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told me, adding that the president’s push to require tech companies to pay for their own power and water resources has protected residents. Some Republicans have bristled at the president’s rhetorical approach, even if they agree with him on the substance. “I actually think Trump is right, but, as usual, his language gets in the way of what he wants to accomplish,” Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and the former communications director of the Republican National Committee, told me. Heye acknowledged that voter “wariness” about AI is ubiquitous but said that politicians who are now trying to recant their earlier support for data centers are projecting a sense of fear rather than leadership. “Voters can smell that,” he said. A Pew Research Center poll released last month found that just over half of Americans feel more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI in daily life, up from 37 percent in 2021. Voters have expressed concerns that the fast-advancing technology could replace human jobs, drive up energy costs, and pollute the environment. The AI industry has sullied its own image with “the worst sales pitch in the history of sales pitches,” said Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, who recently proposed a 100 percent federal tax on any state or local incentives provided to data centers. Speaking at the Ohio Energy Affordability Summit earlier this month, Moreno said that voters are angry and worried that “these data centers are going to come into our community and take our water and pollute our environment. They’re going to raise our electricity prices. They’re going to eventually put us out of work—and our taxpayer dollars are going to support the construction of these things.” The latest warnings about superintelligence and human extinction have spurred even the largest AI companies to call on Congress to step in quickly to regulate their industry before it is no longer possible (or, perhaps, before smaller competitors can get a foothold). Amodei said that the government has a role to play in helping slow down AI development, including by implementing regulations “focused on keeping capabilities in balance with safety.” The government can also mediate or facilitate discussions between companies to help them set safety standards and embed third-party evaluators. Amodei wrote that he agrees with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and that the U.S. should take measures that include not selling powerful AI chips to China. “Companies and the US government should cooperate to make these steps as effective as possible,” Amodei wrote. In a post Wednesday, OpenAI’s chief global-affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that the U.S. is facing a brief opportunity to create guardrails around AI development “before AI capabilities outpace the institutions responsible for governing them.” He said that OpenAI now supports several state regulations on the technology that the company had opposed just months ago. “The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments. The United States needs mandatory, capability-based national regulation that can evolve as the technology does,” Lehane wrote. Sanders told me that he is hopeful that at least some politicians will be willing to work across the aisle out of a sense of self-preservation. He said that his goal over the coming days is to get lawmakers to put pressure on Trump ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month, with the hope of encouraging Trump to focus on negotiating a kind of arms treaty with China to rein in AI advancement globally. But getting Trump’s attention in this political environment may be a challenge in and of itself. On Wednesday, the president spent nearly two hours speaking about his agenda and a wide range of issues at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas. Trump promised to pay every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 if Republicans hold both houses of Congress, and he told a fictional story about a Democratic Senate candidate vomiting after eating barbecue. He also suggested that the Strait of Hormuz should be renamed the “Trump Strait.” He did not mention AI.

items.title: Gov’t must focus on quality everywhere, not categorisation of public schools – Ben Boakye
items.description: Executive Director of the Africa Centre for Energy Policy (ACEP), Ben Boakye, has urged the government to focus on improving the quality of education in every senior high school rather than placing too much emphasis on the categorisation of schools. He said the current debate around the Senior High School (SHS) placement system should not be centred solely on which schools are classified as Category A, B or C, but on ensuring that all schools have the teachers, facilities and support needed to provide quality education. Speaking on JoyNews ‘ Newsfile on Saturday, September 12, during a discussion on the SHS placement crisis, Mr Boakye said there are short, medium and long-term issues that must be addressed. “There are short-term, medium-term, and long-term issues that have to be addressed,” he said. However, he questioned the value of maintaining a system where schools are placed into categories without doing enough to improve the quality of education across the board. “But I don’t see how we should lock ourselves into categories of schools and not improve quality of education at all levels,” he said. “I don’t think it makes sense.” Mr Boakye said the government should instead ensure that schools across the country have capable teachers who can provide students with the education and training they need. “We really have to make sure that the teachers that are, you know, assigned to all the schools can deliver,” he said. He acknowledged that parents and students may continue to have strong preferences for certain schools, including emotional attachments to particular institutions. “As for people categorizing and emotional attachment to schools, we can leave them to do that,” he said. However, he said such preferences should not determine the government’s education priorities. According to him, the focus should be on ensuring that every secondary school is capable of delivering the skills and knowledge students need to become productive members of society. “But the government should focus on making sure that every secondary school can deliver the kind of training and learning that students uh will need to build the human capital that we actually need,” Mr Boakye said. The ACEP Executive Director also called for a broader approach to assessing students, particularly at the Junior High School (JHS) level. He said the education system should prioritise ensuring that every child gets the opportunity to attend school and develop their abilities, rather than placing excessive emphasis on grades obtained at the JHS level. “The problem we really need to face for me is that we need to make sure that every kid goes to school,” he said. “We shouldn’t be too busy about grades and judging kids by their grades at JHS level.” Mr Boakye said that children develop at different rates and that strong performance at the JHS level does not necessarily determine how well a student will perform later in life. “Because kids, you know, develop at different paces, right?” he said. “Some will do better at JHS. They go to university, they do better than those who did well in JHS.” He therefore called for an education system that gives students equal opportunities to develop regardless of their early academic performance. “So we need to push to give people equal opportunity and ability to grow to become better citizens of our state,” he said. Mr Boakye said improving the quality of education across all secondary schools should be a shared priority, particularly because most teachers are graduates and should be supported to deliver effectively. “And I think that should be the priority for all of us in making sure that the schools can deliver,” he said. He added that effective monitoring could also help ensure that schools are meeting the required standards. “The teachers, and most of them are all graduates in the schools. In some instances, just monitoring to make sure that the schools deliver,” he said. This comes amid an ongoing debate over the challenges facing the Computerised School Selection and Placement System (CSSPS), including strong competition for places in some of the country’s most sought-after senior high schools.

items.title: Tanko Computer backs comprehensive review of 1992 Constitution
items.description: Deputy Director of Elections and Information Technology of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Rashid Tanko Computer, says Ghana’s 1992 Constitution is due for a comprehensive review to address shortcomings that have emerged after more than three decades of operation. He said the government is committed to the constitutional reform process and believes several recommendations previously outlined in a government White Paper have already informed its current position. Mr Tanko Computer said the Constitution has “come of age” and must be reviewed to make Ghana’s democratic and administrative arrangements more responsive to current realities, he said on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday. “Government means business in trying to give us a very revised Constitution because if you look at our Constitution, the one we have operated for almost 30 years plus, it has come of age. It needs to be revised; we need to review it properly and look at it.” Mr Tanko Computer said any proposed changes to local government administration must take into account the fact that Ghana operates a unitary presidential executive system, rather than a federal system. His comments come amid discussions about proposals for the election of Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), including calls for political parties to participate openly in such elections. He argued that arrangements of that nature could function more effectively within a federal system, where powers and responsibilities are constitutionally distributed between central and sub-national governments. “What TUC is talking of can work effectively under federalism, which we are not operating. This country is not under federal system,” he said. According to him, Ghana’s current political structure requires careful consideration of the relationship between the central government and local authorities before introducing reforms that could create competing political centres. Mr Tanko Computer warned that allowing political parties to field candidates in MMDCE elections could result in a situation where the President belongs to one party while local authorities across an entire region are controlled by the opposition. He used the Ashanti Region to illustrate his concern, suggesting that a government could face difficulties implementing national policies and coordinating the distribution of resources if opposition-affiliated DCEs controlled local administrations across the region. “If you go all out and say everybody should go and contest as MMDCEs, political parties, we open the floodgates,” he said. He argued that a President elected on a national mandate would have responsibility for the equitable distribution of resources and the security of the state, but could encounter challenges if local political leadership was dominated by an opposing party. “You have your opponent go and put up candidates in the Ashanti Region and the whole of Ashanti Region have NPP DCEs sitting up there,” he said. Mr Tanko Computer said such a scenario could create tensions in the coordination of government and potentially raise security concerns. “You can imagine the kind of security threat that we are going to have in this country. That is the challenge,” he added.

items.title: 2026 SHS placement crisis was caused by changes to established model – Former Dept. GES Director
items.description: Former Deputy Director-General of the Ghana Education Service (GES), Dr Kwabena Bempah Tandoh, has attributed the difficulties surrounding the 2026 Senior High School (SHS) placement exercise to changes made to the established placement model. Speaking on JoyNews ’ Newsfile on Saturday, Dr Tandoh, who is also spokesperson for the NPP Policy Committee on Education, said the controversy was largely the result of changes to student selection, eligibility requirements and the number of Category A schools candidates could choose. His comments come amid public concern over reports involving approximately 55,000 candidates in the 2026 placement exercise. Dr Tandoh said Ghana’s secondary school placement system had historically been based on two key considerations: student choice and the availability of places in schools. He explained that before the 1987 education reforms, pupils completed primary education and sat the Common Entrance examination, after which secondary schools admitted students based largely on their preferred schools and the capacity available. The 1987 reforms introduced the JSS and SSS structure, which later evolved into the current JHS and SHS system. However, the challenge of limited spaces remained, making grading, merit and school capacity important components of admission. According to Dr Tandoh, the introduction of the Computerised School Selection and Placement System (CSSPS) in 2005 modernised the process by using computers to replicate the work previously done manually by school authorities. He stressed, however, that computerisation did not eliminate cut-off points because schools could only admit students according to their available capacity. Dr Tandoh said the introduction of Free SHS in 2017 was accompanied by a deliberate effort to expand access to secondary education. He noted that from 2017 to 2025, students who failed both English Language and Mathematics were generally the ones excluded from progression to SHS, with the number remaining within a relatively narrow range. He cited 10,184 students in 2024 and 13,919 in 2025 as examples. However, he said the eligibility rule was changed in 2026 without adequate communication, consultation and collaboration with stakeholders. According to him, this contributed to the initial decision to classify 54,985 candidates as disqualified, before the Ministry of Education adjusted its position about 48 hours later and allowed the affected students to pursue self-placement. Dr Tandoh argued that the reversal itself demonstrated the uncertainty created by the change in policy. The former GES official also disputed the suggestion that Ghana’s placement difficulties were primarily caused by an overall shortage of SHS places. He cited figures indicating that 859,828 places were available, while the number of candidates requiring placement was about 623,000. He further pointed to claims that 1,132 infrastructure projects were undertaken between 2019 and 2025 to increase school capacity. For Dr Tandoh, the figures indicate that the fundamental problem is not necessarily a lack of spaces nationwide, but the concentration of demand on particular schools. “Choice and space availability” therefore remain central to understanding the placement challenge, he said. Dr Tandoh identified the decision to allow students to select two Category A schools as one of the major changes that placed additional pressure on the system. Under the previous arrangement, he said, a candidate could select only one Category A school, with other choices coming from Categories B and C. Allowing two Category A choices meant that the same limited number of places attracted significantly more applications. He said Category A schools had only about 76,417 available places, yet approximately 313,000 students selected Category A schools. He described the change as poorly thought through, arguing that it created a substantial gap between demand and available capacity. Dr Tandoh also criticised the communication that students with aggregates between six and 10 could access Category A schools. He said the policy created expectations among students and parents without sufficiently accounting for the number of candidates likely to achieve those grades compared with the limited number of Category A places. Dr Tandoh stressed that admission to SHS must ultimately balance choice with merit. Using Presbyterian Boys’ Secondary School (Presec) as an example, he explained that a school could declare 1,300 vacancies overall while having only 200 places in a particular programme such as Science. If 5,000 candidates selected that programme as their first choice, only the highest-performing 200 could be admitted because the school could not exceed its available capacity. The remaining candidates would then be considered for their subsequent choices, depending on the placement rules. Dr Tandoh therefore maintained that choosing a school does not guarantee admission to it, particularly where demand substantially exceeds capacity. He argued that the 2026 crisis was ultimately driven by changes to the placement model, increased pressure on Category A schools and inadequate communication of the new rules, rather than simply a shortage of school infrastructure. He called for greater consistency in education policy and stronger consultation with stakeholders before major changes are introduced to the SHS placement system.

items.title: GMet forecasts thunderstorms, rain across parts of Ghana tonight
items.description: The Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) has forecast thunderstorms and rain of varying intensities across parts of the country this evening and into the night. In its evening forecast for Saturday, September 12, GMet said mostly cloudy conditions would prevail in other parts of the country. The agency further warned that mist and fog patches are likely to develop early Sunday morning over coastal, forest and mountainous areas. It also said slight to moderate rain is expected over some coastal and forest areas during the morning hours. GMet also reported that the state of the sea is currently rough and urged the public to stay safe as the weather conditions persist.

items.title: GETFund to allocate GH¢250m to expand Category A SHS infrastructure
items.description: The Minister for Education, Haruna Iddrisu, says he has asked the Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFUND) to allocate GH¢250 million this year to expand infrastructure in Category A senior high schools. According to him, the additional investment will help ease pressure on some of the country’s most sought-after schools, which have experienced a sharp rise in student numbers under the Free Senior High School (Free SHS) programme. Speaking on JoyNews ‘ Newsfile on Saturday, September 12, during a discussion on the SHS placement crisis, Mr Iddrisu said he had already discussed the matter with the GETFUND administrator. “I’m also happy to note that I requested, and I had a discussion with the administrator of GETFUND, that he should make an allocation of 250 million this year,” he said. The minister said the funds would be used to expand facilities in Category A schools, while other infrastructure needs would be addressed through the government’s planned World Bank-funded programme. “Then we can expand the facilities in the Category A schools, while the World Bank focuses on other areas,” Mr Iddrisu said. Mr Iddrisu said the planned expansion would cover some of the country’s leading senior high schools, including Achimota School, Wesley Girls’ High School, Wesley College, Presbyterian Boys’ Secondary School (PRESEC) and Prempeh College. He said the government intends to provide additional classrooms and accommodation facilities to help the schools cope with increasing enrolment. “We can start classrooms, two dormitories, male and female, at Achimota, Wesley Girls, Holy Child, Presec, and Prempeh,” he said. The minister’s comments come amid growing concerns over the ability of some Category A schools to accommodate the number of students seeking admission. The pressure has contributed to the difficulties experienced by some students and parents during the Computerised School Selection and Placement System (CSSPS) process, particularly where demand for places far exceeds available capacity. Mr Iddrisu also defended the government’s decision to increase investment in community-based secondary education as part of a longer-term solution to the placement challenges. He said President John Mahama had directed him to pursue the construction of model community day schools in selected areas. “That’s what I said; the President has directed me. For instance, in Nima, Ayawaso, we’ll build a model community day school,” he said. Mr Iddrisu said the project would also form part of the government’s broader infrastructure plans, adding that President Mahama would cut the sod for the $300 million project once procurement processes have been completed. “That is where President Mahama will cut the sword for the Star J 300 million U.S. dollar project, as soon as we are done with procurement,” he said. He also announced plans for special education facilities in other parts of the country. “We’ll build special education in Ho, and then Sunyani, and we are considering one for Kintampo,” he said. Beyond the immediate placement crisis, Mr Iddrisu said Ghana needs to reconsider how resources are distributed across the education sector. He said he had taken note of suggestions from education experts, including Professor Adei and the late Professor Gyaama, who he said had written extensively on education. “We are at it, but I take the advice from Professor Adei, and he and other persons, including the late Professor Jampa, wrote extensively on education,” he said. The minister said that Ghana is spending too much on secondary education at the expense of foundational learning at the basic level. “But, again, Ghana, we are spending too much on secondary education,” he said. “That is the major damage that privatisation did to Ghana’s education system.” Mr Iddrisu said education resources should instead be directed towards foundational learning, particularly literacy and numeracy. “Everywhere in the world, focus, resources, and investment must be aligned to foundational learning, basic education, where literacy and numeracy are gained.” “If a child gets literacy right, that child is more likely to succeed,” he said. The minister also pointed to the government’s spending on the school feeding programme as an example of investment at the basic education level. He said the government currently spends about GH¢3.4 billion on school feeding. “But we are spending 3.4 billion on school feeding, in the name of pre-senior high school,” he said. He added that, despite the broader concerns about education spending, the school feeding programme remains a positive intervention. “At least, that’s a good thing we have also done as a government,” Mr Iddrisu said.

items.title: From dream homes to mortgage plans: JoyNews-Repubic Bank Habitat Fair closes Day 2 on a high
items.description: The dream of owning a home took centre stage at the JoyNews–Republic Bank Habitat Fair on Saturday, September 12, as prospective homeowners turned up in numbers to seek answers, explore options and engage experts in Ghana’s housing sector. Day Two of the three-day fair at the Marina Mall in Accra ended with a strong turnout, with visitors moving from one exhibition stand to another as they explored everything from mortgage financing and real estate to construction, interior décor, security and renewable energy. For many of the visitors, the fair was an opportunity to move beyond simply thinking about owning a home and begin understanding what it takes to make that dream a reality. Questions around financing featured prominently, with prospective homeowners engaging representatives of Republic Bank Ghana on mortgage facilities, eligibility, repayment arrangements and the requirements for purchasing, building or renovating a home. The bank’s representatives also interacted with salaried workers, self-employed professionals, entrepreneurs and business owners seeking information on financing options suited to their individual circumstances. But financing was only one part of the conversations. Visitors also sought advice from property and construction professionals, explored home improvement solutions and checked out products designed to make homes more comfortable, secure and energy efficient. The fair brought together businesses and professionals from across the housing and property industry, giving patrons the opportunity to compare products and services and get direct answers from industry experts. For exhibitors, the interactions provided an opportunity to connect directly with people at different stages of their homeownership journey, while visitors gained practical information to help them make more informed decisions. With Day Two now concluded, the JoyNews–Republic Bank Habitat Fair enters its final day on Sunday, September 13. The final day is expected to provide another opportunity for prospective homeowners, property investors and members of the public to engage exhibitors and experts and explore solutions to their housing needs. – Photo Credit: David Andoh

items.title: Afoko: Women’s inclusion key to NPP’s electoral comeback
items.description: New Patriotic Party (NPP) National Chairmanship aspirant Awentami Paul Afoko has called for greater inclusion of women in the party’s administrative structures, describing them as critical to its organisational strength and electoral fortunes. Speaking to party delegates as he campaigns for the party’s top administrative position, Mr Afoko said women play vital roles as organisers, communicators, business leaders, professionals, farmers, traders, caregivers and strategists. He described women as the “backbone” of homes, communities and party structures and said their participation must be central to any effort to renew and reposition the NPP. “To the women of our party and of Ghana, I say this: no serious renewal of the NPP can take place without women at the centre. If you educate a man, you educate an individual, but if you educate a woman, you educate a whole nation,” he stated. Mr Afoko said, if elected National Chairman, he would make women’s participation a central component of the party’s organisation and policy-making. He said his priorities would include expanding women’s roles in party organisation, policy engagement, fundraising, communication, mobilisation and leadership development. “The NPP cannot recapture power without women. Ghana cannot prosper without women. Women’s inclusion is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for electoral success and national development,” he reiterated. According to Mr Afoko, meaningful participation by women in decision-making and policy development would help the NPP rebuild trust and strengthen its connection with communities across the country. He said women’s experiences and contributions across Ghana’s economic and social sectors should be reflected in the party’s policies as it seeks to revitalise its structures and broaden its appeal ahead of future elections. His comments come as the NPP prepares to renew its leadership and reassess its strategies following its defeat in the 2024 general elections.

items.title: Météo | Orages, pluies locales et vents forts annoncés
items.description: L'Institut national de la météorologie (INM) annonce une nuit marquées par des vents et des pluies orageuses dans différentes régions du pays. ​Des cellules orageuses accompagnées de pluies localement intenses toucheront les régions ouest avant de s'étendre progressivement vers le sud-est, précise l'INM, en ajoutant que des vents relativement forts sont attendus près des côtes, sur les hauteurs et dans le sud où il provoquera des phénomènes locaux de sable. Modéré ailleurs, il dépassera toutefois temporairement 70 km/h en rafales sous les orages. Pour les températures nocturnes, celles-ci seront comprises entre 17 °C et 22 °C sur le nord et les hauteurs, entre 23 °C et 28 °C sur le reste du pays, et atteignant jusqu'à 32 °C dans l'extrême sud. Y. N. L’article Météo | Orages, pluies locales et vents forts annoncés est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: La Mauritanie condamne fermement les attaques menées contre des installations vitales saoudiennes
items.description: Le gouvernement mauritanien a fermement condamné les attaques qui ont visé des installations vitales en Arabie saoudite, dans un communiqué publié ce samedi par le ministère des Affaires étrangères. Le ministère mauritanien a exprimé « sa condamnation ferme des attaques qui ont visé l’oléoduc Est-Ouest et les installations vitales du Royaume d’Arabie saoudite frère » et exprimé « la solidarité totale de la République islamique de Mauritanie avec le Royaume d’Arabie saoudite frère ». Le ministère a également souligné « le rejet catégorique par la Mauritanie de tous les actes visant les installations civiles et vitales, et menaçant la sécurité, la stabilité et l’intégrité territoriale de l’Arabie saoudite ». Il a réaffirmé « son soutien au Royaume face aux différentes menaces qui pèsent sur sa sécurité et sa stabilité ».
